name: Nature Pictures and the Pain of Social Ostracism (recall + photo viewing)
description:
Faithful replication of Study 4 of Yang, Wang, Passmore, Zhang, Zhu & Cai (2020), "Viewing nature scenes reduces the pain of social ostracism", The Journal of Social Psychology 161(2), 197–215. Rebuilt from the authors' own Study 4 materials on OSF (osf.io/6xv3t, CC BY 4.0): recall instructions, manipulation check, the three slide sets of 14 photos (nature, urban scenes, neutral objects) and the questionnaire package.

What participants do: (1) write at least five lines about a painful experience of being refused or ostracized (or, in the control condition, an experience of being accepted or welcomed); (2) rate five manipulation-check statements (1–7); (3) as a separate "Perception of Pictures and Well-being Inventory" study, view 14 photos one at a time at their own pace, at least 5 s each, imagining being immersed in the scene; (4) rate 18 emotion words right now (1–5), eight need-satisfaction statements about the recalled event (1–5) and four pain words (1–10); (5) age and sex. Recall condition (2) and picture set (3) are assigned at random and independently: 2 × 3 between subjects. Viewing time per photo is recorded.

Analysis as in the paper: compare picture conditions on state social pain (mean of the 4 pain words), affect balance (positive minus negative words) and retrospective need satisfaction (reverse rejected, outsider, meaningless, non-existent), within the ostracism condition and across the 2 × 3 design. The paper reports lower social pain and higher affect balance after nature photos across four studies (meta-analytic d = 0.58).

Differences from the original study: (1) online in English; the original ran with Chinese university students using paper sheets, PowerPoint slides and a wjx.cn questionnaire, with a student ID and a small gift, both left out. (2) "At least five lines" is enforced as at least 250 characters. (3) The inclusion instruction in the OSF file says "painful life experiences where you were accepted"; "painful" is dropped here. (4) The paper text was not available to us, so the 2 × 3 cell structure follows the Study 4 materials (one exclusion and one inclusion recall version, three photo sets); the Study 4 package has no self-esteem scale, so none is included. (5) Photos keep the original slide order; a short debriefing is added at the end.

Source and credit: photos and wording come from the authors' OSF project and are used with credit; the template is taken down if the authors object.
author: Yang, Wang, Passmore, Zhang, Zhu & Cai

elements.name: consent
elements.title: I agree to participate in this study.

elements.name: recall
elements.title: Recall task
elements.description: { condition: 'exclusion' | 'inclusion', text, chars, seconds } — random assignment to recall a painful experience of being refused or ostracized (exclusion) or an experience of being accepted or welcomed (inclusion), written in at least five lines (here: at least 250 characters).

elements.name: manip_check

rows.text: I can well recall the experience

elements.title: The five statements described your possible feelings when you are recalling the experience of being ostracized. Please indicate your agreement on a seven point scale, according your feelings of the experiences you recalled.
elements.description: Manipulation check, 1–7 (Completely disagree … Completely agree). Ostracism = mean of MC1, MC2 and reversed MC3 (8 − MC3); recall vividness = mean of MC4, MC5.

elements.name: pictures
elements.title: Picture viewing
elements.description: { condition: 'nature' | 'urban' | 'neutral', views: [{ file, ms }], total_s } — random assignment (independent of the recall condition) to one of three sets of 14 photos from the authors' Study 4 slides (folders nature, urban, neutral), shown one at a time in the original slide order at the participant's own pace; Next unlocks after 5 s (the original asked to watch each picture at least 5 s and imagine being immersed in the scene). ms = time on each picture.

elements.name: affect
elements.title: Measure #1. This scale consists of a number of words that describe different feelings and emotions. For each word, please indicate to what extent you feel this emotion RIGHT NOW.

columns.text: Very slightly or Not at all

elements.description: 18 emotion words, 1–5. PA1–PA9 positive, NA1–NA9 negative; affect balance = mean(PA) − mean(NA).

elements.name: needs

rows.text: I felt I had control over the course of the interaction

elements.title: Measure #2. This scale consists of eight statements that describe different psychological reactions to the event you recalled. For each statement, with regard to the event you recalled, please indicate to what extent you felt:

columns.text: Very slightly or Not at all

elements.description: Retrospective need satisfaction about the recalled event, 8 items, 1–5; items ending in R are reversed (6 − x) before averaging.

elements.name: pain
elements.title: Measure #3. This questionnaire provides you with a list of words that describe some of the different qualities of pain. Please choose the number that best describes the intensity of each of the pain you feel right now about the event you recalled. Use 1 if the word does not describe your pain.
elements.description: State social pain, 4 pain words, 1–10 (none … Worst possible); social pain = mean of the 4.

elements.title: What is your age in years (how old are you)?

config.description: Faithful replication of Study 4 of Yang, Wang, Passmore, Zhang, Zhu & Cai (2020), The Journal of Social Psychology 161(2):197–215, rebuilt from the authors' own Study 4 materials on OSF (6xv3t, CC BY 4.0). Participants recall and write about an experience of being ostracized (or, in the control condition, accepted), answer a five-item manipulation check, then view 14 photos of nature, urban scenes or neutral objects at their own pace (at least 5 s each), and report their current emotions, retrospective need satisfaction about the recalled event and state social pain. 2 × 3 between-subjects design.

paper.title: Viewing nature scenes reduces the pain of social ostracism
